P.w: 'Kyoto's Kitchen' — a narrow five-block covered street of more than a hundred food shops (the first opened around 1310): pickles, fresh yuba, dashi-maki tamago, seasonal Kyoto produce and knives.
Lantern-lit lane of teahouses and restaurants squeezed between the Kamo River and Kiyamachi — one of Kyoto's five geisha districts, with summer kawayuka dining platforms over the river.
Head temple of the Ōtani branch of Jōdo Shinshū near Kyoto Station; its Goeidō founder's hall is Kyoto's largest wooden structure. Free to enter.
Hiroshi Hara's 1997 glass-and-steel station building, built for the city's 1,200th anniversary — the giant atrium staircase climbs to a free rooftop skyway with city views.
The 131-metre tower opposite Kyoto Station, the city's tallest structure; the observation deck at 100 m gives a 360° view to Osaka on clear days.
JR West's museum (2016) by Umekōji Park with more than 50 retired trains, from steam locomotives in a working roundhouse to shinkansen; closed Wednesdays.
Japan's first manga museum, in a 1929 elementary-school building by Karasuma-Oike Station, with some 300,000 items and walls of manga you can pull down and read.
Head shrine of the thousands of Inari shrines across Japan, dedicated to the god of rice and sake by the Hata clan in the 8th century — tunnels of thousands of vermilion torii climb Mount Inari.
Museum of Gekkeikan, one of Fushimi's largest and oldest brewers, in a renovated 1909 sake storehouse beside the Horikawa canal — traditional brewing tools and a tasting at the end.
Site of Toyotomi Hideyoshi's retirement castle on Momoyama hill, around which the Fushimi sake town grew; today's keep is a modern reconstruction.
The Fushimi boat-inn where Sakamoto Ryōma was attacked by shogunate police in 1866; rebuilt after the 1868 Battle of Toba–Fushimi and open to visitors with Bakumatsu relics.
Willow-lined Horikawa canal quarter of storehouses and some 20–40 breweries drawing on Fushimi's soft spring water — one of Japan's great sake towns; tastings and canal boat rides.
Eastern Kyoto's hillside temple, famous for the wooden terrace with a view over the city; part of the UNESCO 'Historic Monuments of Ancient Kyoto'.
One of Kyoto's best-preserved historic districts — narrow lanes, wooden buildings and merchant shops on the 20–30 minute walk from Kiyomizu-dera to Yasaka Shrine.
Gion's great shrine, home of the Gion Matsuri every July for over a thousand years; busiest at cherry-blossom time beside Maruyama Park.
Public park next to Yasaka Shrine; in early April Kyoto's most popular (and most crowded) hanami spot under the weeping cherry.
Kyoto's most famous geisha district, between Yasaka Shrine and the Kamo River — ochaya teahouses where geiko and maiko entertain.
Founded 1606 by Nene in memory of Toyotomi Hideyoshi; a tsukiyama pond garden of man-made hills, pine and maple. Its sub-temple Entoku-in adds two more Zen gardens.
Head temple of the Jōdo (Pure Land) sect; its Sanmon, 24 m tall and 50 m wide, is the largest wooden temple gate in Japan (early 1600s).
Tendai monzeki temple whose head priests were traditionally imperial; houses the National Treasure painting of the Blue Cetaka (Ao Fudō) and a garden attributed to Sōami.

P.ad: Komatsu-chō (south of Gion), Higashiyama-ku, Kyoto, Japan
P.w: Founded 1202 — the oldest Zen temple in Kyoto, ranked third of the city's five great Zen temples, just south of Gion.
The five-storey Yasaka Pagoda rising over the Higashiyama lanes on the walk up to Kiyomizu-dera.
One of the Kyoto Gozan (five great Zen temples), founded in the 13th century; its Tsūten-kyō bridge over a maple valley is one of Kyoto's most famous autumn-leaf views.
Founded in 951 by the itinerant monk Kūya — the 17th temple of the Saigoku Kannon pilgrimage — in Rokuhara, the old Heike warrior quarter; its Kūya statue shows tiny Buddhas issuing from his mouth.
One of Japan's four national museums, in the Higashiyama temple district opposite Sanjūsangen-dō; Kyoto's major collection of pre-modern Japanese and Asian art.
The 120-metre hall of 1266 (National Treasure) housing 1,001 standing Thousand-armed Kannon statues, flanked by Fūjin and Raijin.

Head temple of the Chisan school of Shingon Buddhism, opposite the Kyoto National Museum; known for its early-Edo pond garden and Momoyama-period Hasegawa school screen paintings that are National Treasures.
Imperial family temple ('Mitera') whose origin traces to the 820s–830s, with imperial mausolea in its wooded precinct below Tōfuku-ji; head of the Sennyū-ji branch of Shingon.
Walled Rinzai Zen complex of some two dozen sub-temples — one of the best places in Japan to see a range of Zen gardens and tea culture.
Head of the shrines to the scholar Sugawara no Michizane — students pray here before exams; famous for its plum grove and its monthly flea market on the 25th.
Daitoku-ji sub-temple famed for its maple-lined bamboo approach and moss garden — one of Kyoto's best autumn-colour spots.
Kyoto's oldest geiko district, by Kitano Tenmangū in the Nishijin weaving quarter; its geiko and maiko serve at the shrine's Baikasai plum tea ceremony every 25 February.
Shrine north of Daitoku-ji prayed to for a fortunate marriage ('tama-no-koshi'); at its east gate two rival shops have grilled aburi-mochi rice cakes for centuries.
Shrine to Abe no Seimei, the Heian court diviner (onmyōji), marked by star-pentagram crests; a pilgrimage spot for fans of onmyōji fiction.
Ancient shrine near Kitano Tenmangū, long one of Kyoto's classic cherry-blossom (hanami) spots.
The 3 km pine-covered sandbar across Miyazu Bay, one of the 'Three Views of Japan' — viewed upside-down through your legs (matanozoki) from the hilltop parks at either end.
Fishing village of funaya — wooden boathouses with living quarters above, built right over the water around Ine Bay; best seen from a bay cruise.
Ōhara's great Tendai temple, its origins traced to the monk Saichō: moss gardens with small jizō statues under maples, at its finest in mid-November.
Small Ōhara temple near Sanzen-in, viewed 'like a picture frame' from the tatami room with matcha — its centrepiece is a carefully pruned 700-year-old pine.
Mountain temple on Mount Kurama, legendary training ground of the young warrior Minamoto no Yoshitsune; a forest trail crosses the ridge down to Kibune.
Shrine to the god of water up the Kibune valley, its stone steps lined with red lanterns; summer visitors dine on kawadoko platforms over the river below.
Shingon temple founded in 781, up a few hundred stone steps in the Takao maple valley — one of Kyoto's three classic autumn-leaf gorges; throw clay kawarake discs off the cliff for luck.
Arashiyama's 'Moon-Crossing Bridge' over the Katsura River — a landmark since the Heian period, last rebuilt in the 1930s, framed by the forested Arashiyama hills.
The roughly 400-metre path through towering bamboo between Tenryū-ji's north gate and Nonomiya Shrine — go at dawn to beat the crowds.
Silent-film star Ōkōchi Denjirō's hillside villa at the top of the bamboo grove — gardens, teahouses and a matcha with views over Kyoto.
Sagano temple holding some 8,000 stone Buddhas and statues for the souls of the dead, with its own small bamboo grove; candle-lit Sentō Kuyō in August.
A ten-minute hike up from just south of Togetsukyō to a hilltop where dozens of Japanese macaques roam freely, with a view over Kyoto.
At the far end of Sagano, a temple of 1,200 moss-softened stone rakan statues, each carved by a different amateur sculptor with its own expression.
Emperor Saga's 9th-century detached palace turned Shingon temple, beside the Ōsawa Pond — one of Japan's oldest surviving garden ponds and a moon-viewing spot.
Small shrine in the bamboo grove with a rare black (unbarked) torii, where imperial princesses purified themselves before serving at Ise; appears in The Tale of Genji.
One of Kyoto's oldest shrines (701), patron of sake brewers — barrels donated by breweries line the grounds — with Shigemori Mirei's Shōwa-era gardens.
Founded in 603 by the Hata clan — Kyoto's oldest temple — whose Reihōden treasure hall holds the serene Miroku Bosatsu, Japan's first National Treasure sculpture.
Two-kilometre canal-side stone path from Ginkaku-ji to the Nanzen-ji neighbourhood, named for philosopher Nishida Kitarō's daily meditative walk; lined with cherry trees.

Head temple of the Nanzen-ji school of Rinzai Zen at the foot of the Higashiyama hills — the massive Sanmon gate, Hōjō rock garden and the brick Meiji-era Lake Biwa Canal aqueduct running through the grounds.
Jōdo temple north of Nanzen-ji, among Kyoto's most famous autumn-colour spots with evening illuminations in November; known for its 'looking-back' Amida statue.
Shrine built in 1895 for the 1,100th anniversary of the capital, its giant vermilion torii towering over Okazaki; the stroll garden behind is one of Kyoto's best for weeping cherry trees.
Quiet temple just off the Philosopher's Path with a moss-thatched gate and raked sand mounds — the most notable temple on the walk, especially in autumn.

P.n: Kyoto City KYOCERA Museum of Art
P.w: Opened in 1933 as the Enthronement Memorial Museum — Japan's oldest public art museum still in its original building, renovated by Jun Aoki; Okazaki Park.

P.n: National Museum of Modern Art, Kyoto
P.w: Fumihiko Maki-designed national museum facing the KYOCERA across the Heian Jingū approach, strong on Kyoto-school painting and modern ceramics (Kawai Kanjirō).
Statesman Yamagata Aritomo's 1894 villa with a lawn-and-stream garden by Ogawa Jihei borrowing the Higashiyama hills; a nationally designated Place of Scenic Beauty.
Nanzen-ji sub-temple whose crane-and-turtle garden by Kobori Enshū is a Special Place of Scenic Beauty.

Retired Emperor Go-Mizunoo's 1655 hillside villa of three gardens stepped among rice terraces at the foot of Mount Hiei; free Imperial Household Agency tours by reservation; Special Place of Scenic Beauty.
Daitoku-ji sub-temple with one of Japan's finest small dry landscape gardens — a 'river' of white gravel flowing from rock 'mountains'; Special Place of Scenic Beauty.
The 17th-century princely villa often called the pinnacle of Japanese garden and architectural design — teahouses around a stroll-garden pond; Imperial Household Agency tours by reservation.
The emperors' residence until 1868, inside the vast Kyoto Gyoen park; the palace grounds are free to visit without reservation.
Uji's 'flower temple' in the northern hills, founded some 1,200 years ago — vast gardens of azaleas, hydrangeas and lotuses in season.
Head temple of the Ōbaku school of Zen, founded by the Chinese monk Ingen in 1661 in Ming-dynasty Chinese style — and the home of fucha ryōri, Chinese-style vegetarian temple cuisine.
The large park at the heart of old Nara holding Tōdai-ji, Kasuga Taisha, Kōfuku-ji and the National Museum, roamed by more than a thousand free-ranging, bowing sika deer.
National museum of Japanese Buddhist art in Nara Park; its autumn Shōsō-in exhibition of 8th-century imperial treasures is a national event.
Two-part stroll garden (mid-17th century front, 1899 rear) that borrows Tōdai-ji's Nandaimon gate and Mount Wakakusa as scenery.
The grass-covered hill behind Nara Park between Tōdai-ji and Kasuga Taisha, with open views over the city; its slopes are set alight each January in the Yamayaki.
Nara-period temple founded by an empress praying for the ailing emperor; the main hall rings the Yakushi Buddha with twelve clay guardian generals.
Tōdai-ji's hillside hall with a free veranda view over Nara; stage of the Shuni-e (Omizutori) fire rite each March, held every year without a break for over 1,270 years.
Founded in 607 by Prince Shōtoku; its pagoda and Golden Hall are the world's oldest surviving wooden buildings — Japan's first UNESCO World Heritage Site (Buddhist Monuments in the Hōryū-ji Area).
One of Kyoto's oldest Shinto shrines, older than the city itself, with its two sand cones (tatesuna) before the Hosodono hall; UNESCO-listed component 688-001.
Ancient shrine at the meeting of the Kamo and Takano rivers, reached through the Tadasu-no-Mori primeval forest; UNESCO-listed component 688-002.

Founded in 796 as the guardian temple at the old capital's south gate; its five-storey pagoda is Japan's tallest wooden pagoda, and a flea market fills the grounds on the 21st of each month. UNESCO 688-003.
Head temple of Tendai Buddhism, founded on Mount Hiei in 788 and spread across the forested summit above Lake Biwa; UNESCO 688-005 (coordinate is the property centre of a 498 ha precinct).
Vast Shingon temple complex whose five-storey pagoda (951) is the oldest building in Kyoto; Toyotomi Hideyoshi's famous cherry-blossom party was held here. UNESCO 688-006.
Former imperial temple (founded 888) known for its late-blooming Omuro dwarf cherry trees and five-storey pagoda; UNESCO 688-007.
The 11th-century Phoenix Hall pictured on the 10-yen coin, reflected in its Pure Land garden pond; UNESCO 688-008.
Small shrine across the Uji River from Byōdō-in whose main hall is regarded as Japan's oldest surviving shrine building; UNESCO 688-009.
Mountain temple in Toganoo above Takao, keeper of the Chōjū-giga animal scrolls often called Japan's first manga; UNESCO 688-010.
The 'Moss Temple' — a garden carpeted with over a hundred kinds of moss; visits are by advance reservation only. UNESCO 688-011.
Head temple of the Rinzai Tenryū-ji school, founded 1339, with Musō Soseki's Sōgen pond garden borrowing the Arashiyama hills; UNESCO 688-012.
The Golden Pavilion — a gold-leafed Zen reliquary hall over a mirror pond, rebuilt in 1955 after arson; UNESCO 688-013.
The Silver Pavilion, Ashikaga Yoshimasa's retirement villa turned Zen temple, with its raked-sand garden and moss paths at the head of the Philosopher's Path; UNESCO 688-014.
Home of Japan's most famous dry rock garden — fifteen stones on raked gravel; UNESCO 688-015.
Head temple of the Jōdo Shinshū Hongwanji-ha, a short walk from Kyoto Station, with vast Founder's and Amida halls and Momoyama-era gates; UNESCO 688-016.
The Tokugawa shoguns' Kyoto residence (1603), whose Ninomaru Palace 'nightingale floors' chirp underfoot; UNESCO 688-017.
Nara's great temple, whose Daibutsuden houses the 15-metre bronze Great Buddha; UNESCO 'Historic Monuments of Ancient Nara' 870-001.
Fujiwara clan temple whose five-storey pagoda rises over Nara Park, with a National Treasure Hall of Buddhist sculpture including the Ashura statue; UNESCO 870-002.
Vermilion shrine of the Fujiwara famed for its thousands of stone and bronze lanterns, set against the protected Kasugayama Primeval Forest; UNESCO 870-003.
Successor to Asuka-dera, Japan's first full-scale Buddhist temple; some roof tiles date to the 6th century. In the Naramachi old town. UNESCO 870-004.
Seventh-century imperial temple in western Nara whose East Pagoda is one of Japan's oldest; UNESCO 870-005.
Founded in 759 by the Chinese monk Ganjin (Jianzhen); its Golden Hall is the finest surviving Nara-period main hall. UNESCO 870-006.
The excavated site of the 8th-century imperial palace of Heijō-kyō, with the reconstructed Daigokuden and Suzakumon gate; UNESCO 870-007 (coordinate = centre of a 129 ha site).

F.w: Michelin Bib Gourmand udon house that began delivering meals to Gion teahouses and playhouses; queues form before opening for the onion udon heaped with Kyoto's Kujō spring onion.
The Takabashi ramen institution founded in 1947, five minutes' walk from Kyoto Station — the benchmark for Kyoto's soy-pork-bone style.
Michelin Bib Gourmand ramen shop in Ichijōji; the signature soy-sauce ramen uses a dashi of locally raised free-range chicken and water only, finished with a raw soy-sauce kaeshi.
Michelin Bib Gourmand noodle bar hidden, unsigned, in a residential maze of Murasakino; house noodles of Kyoto wheat in a clear seafood-dashi broth.
